title: What is AI?
def: Software that performs tasks which normally need human intelligence — recognizing images, understanding language, making decisions.
note: AI is the umbrella term. Machine learning, LLMs and agents are all specific approaches inside it, not synonyms for it.

title: What is machine learning?
def: A way of building AI where the system learns patterns from data instead of being explicitly programmed with rules.
note: Show it enough labeled examples, and it learns the pattern itself — that's the shift from classic programming to ML.

title: What is an LLM?
def: A Large Language Model — a neural network trained on huge amounts of text, so it can read and generate language.
note: ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini are all products built around an LLM. The LLM is the model; the product is the model plus an interface.

title: What is an AI agent?
def: An LLM that can take actions, not just reply with text — it can call tools, check results and decide what to do next.
note: A plain chatbot only talks. An agent can act: search the web, run code, call an API, then use what it finds to keep going.

title: What is a "model" in AI?
def: The trained system itself — millions or billions of numbers (parameters) that turn an input into an output.
note: "Model" is the generic term; an LLM is one kind of model, specifically one trained on language.

title: What is a prompt?
def: The text you give the model as input — an instruction, a question, or both.
note: Prompting is how you steer a model without changing its underlying weights. Same model, different prompt, different behavior.

title: Training vs inference — what's the difference?
def: Training is when the model learns from data, once, at huge cost. Inference is every time you actually use it afterward.
note: When you chat with a model, you're doing inference. The model's knowledge was fixed back when it was trained.

title: What is a hallucination in AI?
def: When a model states something false or made-up as if it were fact, with no signal that it's unsure.
note: It happens because the model is predicting plausible-sounding text, not looking facts up — confidence and correctness aren't the same thing.

title: Why doesn't the model know yesterday's news?
def: Training stopped on a fixed date, so the model's knowledge stopped there too — anything that happened afterwards was never part of what it learned.
note: It won't reliably notice that a question falls past that line, so anything current has to be handed to it — by a search, a document, or a tool call.

title: What is fine-tuning?
def: Taking a model that's already trained and training it a little further on your own examples, so it picks up your task, tone or format.
note: It teaches behaviour far better than facts — for fresh or private information, retrieval is usually cheaper, faster to update, and easier to check.
code:
examples = [{"prompt": "...", "completion": "..."}, ...]
tuned = finetune(base_model, examples)   # new weights, same architecture

title: Open-weights vs closed models — what's the difference?
def: Open-weights models you can download and run on your own machines; closed models live on the provider's servers and you reach them only through an API.
note: Open-weights isn't open source — you get the numbers, rarely the training data or the code that produced them, and the licence can still restrict what you're allowed to build.

title: Why does AI run on graphics cards?
def: Running a model is billions of small multiplications, and a graphics card was already built to do thousands of them at once — the same maths that shades a 3D scene.
note: The binding constraint is usually memory, not maths — the weights have to fit in the card's own memory, and once they do, generation speed is limited by how fast they can be read back out.

title: Chatbot, copilot, agent — the autonomy ladder
def: Same model underneath, three levels of autonomy — a chatbot answers, a copilot proposes changes you approve, an agent goes and does the work itself.
note: Climbing the ladder isn't a smarter model, it's a wider permission grant — so every rung up needs more guardrails than the one below it.
code:
flowchart LR
    C[Chatbot: answers]:::n --> P[Copilot: you approve each step]:::n --> A[Agent: acts, then reports]:::ok
    classDef n fill:#EFE9FE,stroke:#7C3AED,color:#5B21B6,font-size:13px
    classDef ok fill:#E3F4F1,stroke:#0E9384,color:#0A6A60,font-size:13px

title: What is a multimodal model?
def: A model that takes more than text — images, audio, sometimes video — and turns each of them into tokens it reads alongside your words.
note: Reading a picture and drawing one are separate abilities; plenty of models can describe a photo in detail without being able to generate an image at all.

title: What is a reasoning model?
def: A model trained to work a problem through step by step before it answers — it spends extra tokens thinking, so you wait longer and pay more.
note: That trade pays off on maths, code and multi-step logic; on lookup, summarizing or ordinary chat it mostly buys you latency for the same answer.
code:
Thought: 3 apples cost 1.80, so one is 0.60.
Thought: 7 x 0.60 = 4.20.
Answer: 4.20   <- usually the only part you see

title: Token
def: The smallest chunk of text a model reads or writes — usually a word-piece, not a whole word.
note: Everything is counted, priced and limited in tokens. For English, ~4 characters is about 1 token.
code: tokens = ["token", "izing"]   # "tokenizing" -> 2 tokens, not 1 word

title: Context window
def: The maximum number of tokens a model can hold in view at once — your prompt and its reply combined.
note: Anything outside it is invisible. Overflow means the oldest tokens fall off or must be summarized.
code:
used = prompt_tokens + reply_tokens
assert used <= context_window   # or it overflows

title: Temperature
def: How random the model's sampling is. Low keeps it focused and repeatable; high makes it diverse and creative.
note: Near 0 it's almost deterministic — good for extraction. Raise it for brainstorming.
code: { "temperature": 0.2, "top_p": 1.0 }

title: Chat messages
def: Modern LLM APIs take a list of role-tagged messages, not a single prompt string.
note: system sets behaviour, user asks, assistant answers — and the whole history is resent every turn.

title: Embedding
def: Text turned into a fixed-length vector, so meaning becomes a distance you can measure.
note: Similar meanings land near each other — the basis for search, clustering and retrieval.

title: System prompt
def: A standing instruction that sits at the front of every request and sets the model's role, rules and tone — resent each turn, never shown to the end user.
note: It's a steering tool, not a security boundary — a user or a poisoned tool result can talk the model around it, so nothing secret belongs in there.

title: Top-p / top-k sampling
def: Two ways of cutting the candidate next tokens down before one is drawn: top-k keeps a fixed number, top-p keeps as many as it takes to cover that share of the probability.
note: Temperature reshapes the odds but never rules a token out, while these two do — turn all three at once and you won't know which one changed the output.

title: Few-shot prompting
def: Showing the model a couple of worked examples inside the prompt so it picks up the pattern you want — no training, no fine-tuning, just input.
note: The examples ride along on every call, and the model copies whatever is actually in them, including formatting quirks you never meant to demonstrate.

title: Chain of thought
def: Getting the model to work the problem out in steps before it answers, so each step becomes part of the input that shapes the next one.
note: Reasoning models now do this internally by default, and either way the written steps are a plausible narrative rather than a faithful log — a tidy chain can still end at a wrong answer.

title: Structured output / JSON mode
def: Handing the model a schema along with the request so the reply comes back as JSON your code can parse, instead of prose you have to scrape.
note: Strict modes enforce the shape by constraining what the decoder may emit, so the fields will be there — whether the values are right is still your problem.

title: Streaming
def: Tokens are pushed to the client as they're generated instead of being held back until the reply is finished — the total time barely moves, the waiting does.
note: You can't validate what hasn't arrived yet, and a stream can still fail halfway through, after the user has already read the first half.
code:
for chunk in model.stream(messages):
    print(chunk.text, end="")   # words appear as they're written

title: Max tokens & stop sequences
def: The two limits you set on where a reply ends — a ceiling on how many tokens it may generate, and strings that cut it off the moment they appear.
note: A reply that stops mid-sentence almost always hit the ceiling rather than finishing — check the stop reason the API returns before you start rewriting the prompt.
code: { "max_tokens": 512, "stop": ["Observation:"] }

title: Token pricing
def: Billing counts tokens rather than requests — every token you send and every token the model generates, with the output side normally charged at the higher rate.
note: You pay for output you throw away too, so a reply that fails validation and gets retried costs exactly as much as one you keep.
code: { "usage": { "input_tokens": 1830, "output_tokens": 210 } }

title: Context rot
def: A model can accept a very long prompt without using all of it evenly — the material buried in the middle is the likeliest to be missed.
note: Fitting inside the window is the low bar — accuracy tends to slide as the prompt grows, so trimming what you send is a quality decision, not just a cost one.

title: Self-attention
def: Every token looks at every other token and weighs how relevant it is — that's how context flows through the model.
note: Query x Key produces the weights; those weights mix the Values. It's the heart of the transformer.
code:
scores  = query @ key.T
weights = softmax(scores)
out     = weights @ value

title: Transformer
def: The architecture behind modern LLMs: stacked self-attention and feed-forward layers, with no recurrence.
note: It processes a whole sequence in parallel, which is why it trains and scales so well.

title: Positional encoding
def: Attention is order-blind on its own, so each token's position is baked into its vector.
note: Without it, "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" would look identical to the model.

title: Softmax
def: Turns raw scores (logits) into a probability distribution that sums to 1.
note: It's the final step that decides how likely each possible next token is.
code: probs = exp(logits) / sum(exp(logits))   # sums to 1

title: Next-token prediction
def: An LLM only ever does one thing: predict the probability of the next token, sample one, and repeat.
note: Everything else — chat, code, reasoning — emerges from doing this well, one token at a time.
code:
logits  = model(tokens)
next_id = sample(softmax(logits), temperature=0.7)

title: KV cache
def: The keys and values attention already computed for earlier tokens, kept in memory and reused — so generating the next token means processing one token, not the whole conversation again.
note: The cache grows with every token and lives in GPU memory, so on a long conversation the thing you run out of first is usually room for the cache, not compute.
code:
k, v = attn_kv(new_token)              # only the new token
cache_k.append(k); cache_v.append(v)   # past work, kept
out = softmax(q @ cache_k.T) @ cache_v

title: Tokenizer (BPE)
def: The fixed vocabulary of word-pieces that text gets chopped into before the model sees anything — byte-pair encoding builds it by repeatedly merging whichever adjacent pair appears most often.
note: It's why letter-level tasks go wrong: the model sees chunks, never characters, so "how many r's" asks it about something it can't actually look at.
code:
merges = [("l","o"), ("lo","w"), ("s","t"), ("e","st")]   # learned by frequency
encode("lowest") -> ["low", "est"]                       # pieces, never letters

title: Decoder-only & causal masking
def: Every token attends only to the tokens before it — the future is masked out, so the model can never peek at the word it's being asked to predict.
note: Drop that mask and you get an encoder — very good at embedding text, useless at generating it left to right — which is why every model you chat with is decoder-only.

title: Pretraining vs post-training
def: Pretraining is the enormous run that learns language from raw text; post-training is the much smaller pass that turns that raw predictor into something which follows instructions.
note: Nearly all the knowledge arrives in pretraining — post-training mostly reshapes behaviour, which is why fine-tuning is a poor way to bolt on facts a model never saw.

title: RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback)
def: One way of doing post-training: people rank competing answers, a reward model learns to predict those rankings, and the LLM is then tuned to score well against it.
note: Optimize too hard against that reward and you get sycophancy — the model learns what raters approve of, and approval isn't the same thing as correctness.

title: Mixture of experts
def: Each layer's feed-forward block is split into many expert sub-networks, and a router sends every token through just a couple of them — huge total capacity, small compute per token.
note: Every expert still has to sit in memory even though only a few fire, so a mixture of experts buys you cheaper compute per token, not cheaper hardware to host it on.
code:
chosen = router.top_k(token, k=2)   # 2 experts of many, per layer
out = sum(w * expert(token) for w, expert in chosen)

title: Quantization
def: Storing the weights at lower numeric precision — fewer bits per number — so the model shrinks and runs faster, while losing surprisingly little quality.
note: Quality doesn't collapse so much as fray — the damage shows up first on the hardest prompts, so a quantized model can pass a quick test and still drift on the long ones.

title: LoRA (low-rank adaptation)
def: Fine-tuning that freezes the original weights and trains a small low-rank pair of matrices beside each one it targets — the reason a fine-tune fits on a single GPU.
note: An adapter is megabytes rather than gigabytes, so one hosted base model can serve many LoRAs swapped in per request, or have one merged back into its weights.
code:
delta = (x @ A) @ B          # A: d x r, B: r x k, r is tiny
y = x @ W_frozen + delta     # only A and B get gradients

title: Distillation
def: Training a small model to imitate a big one's outputs — how a lot of the fast, cheap models you actually use get built.
note: A student inherits the teacher's blind spots along with its strengths, because distillation compresses behaviour that already exists rather than discovering any of its own.

title: Speculative decoding
def: A small fast model drafts the next few tokens and the big model checks them all in one pass, keeping whichever prefix it would have written anyway.
note: Unlike quantization or distillation it costs no quality at all — the accept/reject rule preserves the big model's own output distribution exactly — so the only variable is how often drafts survive.
code:
draft = small(tokens, n=4)        # cheap guesses
ok = big.verify(tokens, draft)    # one pass, all 4
tokens += draft[:ok]              # keep accepted prefix

title: Function calling / tool use
def: The model doesn't run code — it emits a structured request to call a function you defined, and your code runs it.
note: You describe each tool as a schema; the model replies with the name and arguments to invoke. This is the bridge from chat to action.

title: ReAct (reason + act)
def: The model thinks, calls a tool, reads the result, then thinks again — interleaving reasoning with action.
note: Each step is grounded in a real observation instead of one long guessed-at answer.
code:
Thought: I need today's weather.
Action: get_weather("Alicante")
Observation: 29C, clear skies
Thought: Now I can answer.

title: The agent loop
def: An agent is a loop: think, act, observe, repeat — until the goal is met or a step limit is hit.
note: The loop plus tools plus memory is what turns a plain chat model into an agent.
code:
while not done:
    action = model.decide(state)
    result = run(action)
    state  = update(state, result)
    done   = action.is_final

title: Memory
def: Short-term memory is the context window; long-term memory is external storage you retrieve into it.
note: Agents summarize or store past steps so they don't forget once the window fills up.

title: RAG (retrieval-augmented generation)
def: Fetch relevant documents and drop them into the prompt, so the model answers from facts rather than only its training.
note: Cuts hallucination and lets a model use private or fresh data it never saw during training.
code:
docs   = retrieve(query, top_k=4)
prompt = context(docs) + query
answer = model(prompt)

title: MCP (Model Context Protocol)
def: An open standard for connecting models to tools and data through one consistent interface.
note: Write a connector once and any MCP-aware client can use it — a bit like a USB port for tools.

title: What is an AI skill?
def: A folder of instructions and resources — templates, scripts, checklists — that a model reads before doing a task. Packaged know-how, loaded on demand.
note: A skill teaches the model HOW (it reads, then does the work itself); MCP gives it ACCESS to live systems. Runbook vs phone line — full comparison on the MCP vs REST page.
code:
flowchart LR
    F[Skill folder]:::n -->|read into context| M[Model]:::n -->|does the work itself| R[Result]:::ok
    classDef n fill:#EFE9FE,stroke:#7C3AED,color:#5B21B6,font-size:13px
    classDef ok fill:#E3F4F1,stroke:#0E9384,color:#0A6A60,font-size:13px

title: Evals
def: Systematic tests that score model or agent output, so you can tell whether a change actually helped.
note: Without evals you're tuning by vibes; with them, progress becomes measurable.
code: score = sum(check(model(x)) for x in test_set) / len(test_set)

title: What is an agent workflow?
def: A graph of steps an agent system runs through — not one long prompt, but a structured, typed sequence you can inspect and control.
note: This is what separates a serious agent framework from a chat loop: the orchestration itself becomes a first-class, strongly-typed object instead of hidden inside one big prompt.

title: Executors and edges — the building blocks of a workflow
def: An executor is one unit of work in a workflow — an agent or a plain function. An edge is the connection that routes output from one executor to the next.
note: Edges can fan out to run several executors in parallel, fan in to combine their results, or route conditionally based on what came out of the previous step.

title: What is checkpointing in an agent workflow?
def: Saving a workflow's state mid-run, so it can be paused, killed, or crash — and resume later from exactly where it left off, not from the start.
note: This is what makes long-running or expensive agent workflows practical: a multi-hour task survives a restart instead of burning every token again.

title: What is handoff orchestration?
def: A multi-agent pattern where a triage agent routes a request to the right specialist agent, and any specialist can hand the conversation back or sideways if it turns out to be the wrong fit.
note: The developer defines the topology — which agents exist and who can hand off to whom — but the agents themselves decide, in the moment, when a handoff is needed.

title: What is an agent harness?
def: A ready-made shell around a model that turns it into a working coding agent in one step — file access, task tracking, shell execution, and approvals, all pre-wired.
note: Instead of hand-building memory, file tools, and a sandbox yourself, a harness gives you the standard agent scaffolding out of the box.

title: What is agent-to-agent (A2A) communication?
def: A protocol that lets independent agents send each other structured messages, even across different frameworks or programming languages.
note: This is how a .NET agent and a Python agent — built by different teams on different stacks — can still delegate work to one another reliably.

title: Planning vs reacting
def: Two ways to spend an agent's decisions: work the whole task out up front and then execute the plan, or choose one step at a time and let each result steer the next.
note: A plan made up front goes stale the moment reality disagrees with it, and pure step-by-step wanders — most working agents sketch a rough plan, then react inside each step.
code:
flowchart TD
    G[Goal]:::n --> P[Plan the whole task]:::n
    P --> E[Execute the plan]:::ok
    G --> D[Decide one step]:::n
    D --> O[Observe result]:::n
    O --> D
    classDef n fill:#EFE9FE,stroke:#7C3AED,color:#5B21B6,font-size:13px
    classDef ok fill:#E3F4F1,stroke:#0E9384,color:#0A6A60,font-size:13px

title: Reflection / self-critique
def: The agent reads back its own answer, checks it against what was actually asked, and fixes what it finds before handing the work over.
note: It only helps when the critique has something concrete to check against — a test run, a spec, an error message — otherwise the model just re-approves its own mistake more confidently.

title: Subagents
def: Handing a subtask to a separate agent that starts fresh — it sees only the task you give it, not the parent's history — and reports back just its conclusion.
note: The value is in what doesn't come back: the forty files read and the three dead ends stay in the subagent's context, and the parent only pays for the answer.
code:
flowchart TD
    P[Parent agent]:::n -->|subtask| S[Subagent, fresh context]:::n
    S --> E[Reads, tries, discards]:::n
    E -->|conclusion only| R[Parent context stays small]:::ok
    classDef n fill:#EFE9FE,stroke:#7C3AED,color:#5B21B6,font-size:13px
    classDef ok fill:#E3F4F1,stroke:#0E9384,color:#0A6A60,font-size:13px

title: Computer use
def: An agent that drives a real screen the way a person does — it reads what's displayed, moves the pointer, clicks and types.
note: It's the fallback for software with no API: slower and far more brittle than a real tool call, and a redesigned button can break it overnight.

title: Code execution as a tool
def: Instead of one tool per task, give the agent a sandboxed interpreter — it writes the small program a job needs, runs it, and reads the output.
note: The tool that can run anything is also the tool that can break anything, so it belongs in a sandbox with no secrets, no credentials and no network you didn't intend.
code:
code   = model.write_code(task)
result = sandbox.run(code)        # no network, no secrets
answer = model.explain(result)

title: Vector database
def: The store your embeddings live in — you query it by similarity, asking for the vectors nearest to yours, instead of matching a field exactly.
note: Nearest isn't the same as relevant — a top-k query hands back k results whether or not the store holds anything that actually answers the question.

title: Chunking
def: Cutting documents into retrieval-sized pieces before embedding them, because what you get back later is a whole chunk — not a whole file, not one sentence.
note: Too big and every hit drags in irrelevant text; too small and the sentence arrives stripped of the paragraph that explained it.
code:
size, overlap = 800, 100
chunks = [text[i:i + size]
          for i in range(0, len(text), size - overlap)]

title: Reranking
def: A second, slower model re-scores the candidates retrieval returned and reorders them, so only the genuinely relevant ones make it into the prompt.
note: Vector search is cheap and approximate on purpose — retrieve far more than you need, then let the reranker throw most of it away.
code:
candidates = vector_search(query, top_k=50)     # fast, approximate
ranked     = reranker.score(query, candidates)  # slow, careful
context    = ranked[:5]                         # only these reach the prompt

title: Context compaction
def: When the window fills up mid-task, the agent summarizes the run so far and carries on from that summary instead of hitting a wall.
note: Compaction is lossy by design, so anything the rest of the run can't do without belongs in a file or a memory store rather than in a summary that may drop it.
code:
flowchart TD
    R[Run so far]:::n --> F{Window full?}:::n
    F -->|no| C[Keep going]:::ok
    F -->|yes| S[Summarize and drop detail]:::n
    S --> C
    classDef n fill:#EFE9FE,stroke:#7C3AED,color:#5B21B6,font-size:13px
    classDef ok fill:#E3F4F1,stroke:#0E9384,color:#0A6A60,font-size:13px

title: AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md
def: A file checked into the repo that the agent reads at the start of a session — the conventions, the commands that actually work here, and what not to touch.
note: It rots faster than the code does, and a stale command in there gets trusted and run anyway, so prune it as ruthlessly as you would a README.

title: Harness engineering
def: Designing the environment an agent acts inside — its sandbox, its file system access, and the runtime surface it's allowed to touch.
note: A harness decides what's even possible for the agent to attempt. No amount of clever prompting fixes a missing file permission or a shell it can't reach.
code:
flowchart TD
    A[Agent]:::n --> H[Harness]:::n
    H --> SB[Sandbox]:::n
    H --> FS[File system]:::n
    H --> RT[Runtime surface]:::n
    classDef n fill:#EFE9FE,stroke:#7C3AED,color:#5B21B6,font-size:13px

title: Loop engineering
def: Deciding when the agent takes another step and when it stops — the control logic wrapped around think, act, observe.
note: Stop too early and the task is unfinished. Stop too late and you burn tokens on a loop that already found its answer three steps ago.
code:
flowchart TD
    T[Think]:::n --> Ac[Act]:::n --> O[Observe]:::n
    O -->|not done| T
    O -->|done| S([Stop]):::ok
    classDef n fill:#EFE9FE,stroke:#7C3AED,color:#5B21B6,font-size:13px
    classDef ok fill:#E3F4F1,stroke:#0E9384,color:#0A6A60,font-size:13px

title: Context engineering
def: Curating what actually lands in the context window on each turn — pulling in what's relevant, and actively keeping out what isn't.
note: Most 'prompt engineering' problems that show up in production are really context problems: too much irrelevant history, not too few clever words.
code:
flowchart TD
    H[History]:::n --> Sel[Selector]:::n
    Tl[Tool output]:::n --> Sel
    M[Memory]:::n --> Sel
    Sel --> W[Context window]:::ok
    classDef n fill:#EFE9FE,stroke:#7C3AED,color:#5B21B6,font-size:13px
    classDef ok fill:#E3F4F1,stroke:#0E9384,color:#0A6A60,font-size:13px

title: Tool design
def: Writing the tool itself, not just its call schema — an agent's ceiling is what its tools let it do, and its risk is their worst edge case.
note: A tool that fails silently or accepts unchecked input hands the agent a way to cause real damage without anyone actually deciding it should be allowed to.
code:
flowchart TD
    C[Model call]:::n --> Sc[Tool schema]:::n --> V[Validate]:::n --> Ex[Execute]:::ok --> R[Result]:::ok
    classDef n fill:#EFE9FE,stroke:#7C3AED,color:#5B21B6,font-size:13px
    classDef ok fill:#E3F4F1,stroke:#0E9384,color:#0A6A60,font-size:13px

title: Memory architecture
def: The design decisions behind what an agent remembers, for how long, and what it's allowed to forget.
note: Not everything belongs in long-term storage — a well-designed architecture decides what gets promoted from a single run into something durable.
code:
flowchart TD
    C[Context window]:::n -->|fills up| Su[Summarize / evict]:::n
    Su --> L[Long-term store]:::ok
    L -->|retrieve| C
    classDef n fill:#EFE9FE,stroke:#7C3AED,color:#5B21B6,font-size:13px
    classDef ok fill:#E3F4F1,stroke:#0E9384,color:#0A6A60,font-size:13px

title: Orchestration patterns
def: The shape of an agent system — one agent, a planner delegating to workers, or a swarm of peers — and each shape fails differently.
note: A single agent fails by running out of context. A swarm fails by agents stepping on each other's work. Pick the shape for the failure mode you can live with.
code:
flowchart TD
    P[Planner]:::n --> W1[Worker A]:::n
    P --> W2[Worker B]:::n
    classDef n fill:#EFE9FE,stroke:#7C3AED,color:#5B21B6,font-size:13px

title: Guardrails & permissions
def: The checks that run before an agent's action executes, and what happens when the action it wants to take isn't allowed.
note: A guardrail that only logs a violation after the fact isn't a guardrail — it has to be able to block or reroute before the action actually runs.
code:
flowchart TD
    A[Agent action]:::n --> P{Policy check}:::n
    P -->|allowed| E[Execute]:::ok
    P -->|denied| B[Block / ask human]:::warn
    classDef n fill:#EFE9FE,stroke:#7C3AED,color:#5B21B6,font-size:13px
    classDef ok fill:#E3F4F1,stroke:#0E9384,color:#0A6A60,font-size:13px
    classDef warn fill:#FBE7E7,stroke:#B23B3B,color:#8C2323,font-size:13px

title: Evals for agents
def: Scoring an agent's whole trajectory — every step it took — not just whether the final output looks right.
note: Two runs can land on the same correct answer through very different paths, and one of those paths might have touched something it shouldn't have.
code:
flowchart TD
    S1[Step 1]:::n --> S2[Step 2]:::n --> S3[Step N]:::n --> F[Final answer]:::n
    F -.-> Sc[Trajectory score]:::ok
    classDef n fill:#EFE9FE,stroke:#7C3AED,color:#5B21B6,font-size:13px
    classDef ok fill:#E3F4F1,stroke:#0E9384,color:#0A6A60,font-size:13px

title: Human-in-the-loop design
def: Deciding upfront which categories of decision never get delegated to the agent, no matter how confident it is.
note: The line isn't drawn per-request in the moment — it's drawn in the design, before the agent is ever capable of proposing that action.
code:
flowchart TD
    A[Agent proposes]:::n --> D{High-stakes?}:::n
    D -->|no| Au[Auto-run]:::ok
    D -->|yes| H[Human approves]:::warn --> Ex[Execute]:::ok
    classDef n fill:#EFE9FE,stroke:#7C3AED,color:#5B21B6,font-size:13px
    classDef ok fill:#E3F4F1,stroke:#0E9384,color:#0A6A60,font-size:13px
    classDef warn fill:#FBE7E7,stroke:#B23B3B,color:#8C2323,font-size:13px

title: Observability & tracing
def: Recording every step an agent takes — inputs, outputs, timing, tool calls — so a failure deep in a run is inspectable, not a black box.
note: When a 30-step run breaks at step 14, a trace lets you look straight at step 14, instead of re-running the whole thing and guessing where it went wrong.
code:
flowchart TD
    R[Run: steps 1-30]:::n -->|logs every step| T[Trace log]:::n
    T --> J[Jump to step 14]:::ok
    classDef n fill:#EFE9FE,stroke:#7C3AED,color:#5B21B6,font-size:13px
    classDef ok fill:#E3F4F1,stroke:#0E9384,color:#0A6A60,font-size:13px

title: Cost engineering
def: Working out what one request actually costs in tokens before it ships, then treating that number as a budget the prompt, the retrieved context and the model choice all have to fit.
note: Per token the reply usually costs more, but the bill comes from the input — the whole history and every tool result get resent on each turn.
code:
cost = in_tokens * in_rate + out_tokens * out_rate
# out_rate is higher, but in_tokens is the bigger number

title: Model routing
def: Sending each request to the smallest model that can actually handle it, and escalating to a bigger one only when the small one falls short.
note: A bad route doesn't throw an error — it just quietly answers worse, which is why every tier needs its own evals before you trust the router.
code:
flowchart TD
    R[Request]:::n --> C{Simple request?}:::n
    C -->|yes| S[Small model]:::ok
    C -->|no| L[Large model]:::ok
    S -->|not confident| L
    classDef n fill:#EFE9FE,stroke:#7C3AED,color:#5B21B6,font-size:13px
    classDef ok fill:#E3F4F1,stroke:#0E9384,color:#0A6A60,font-size:13px

title: Prompt caching
def: Reusing an identical prompt prefix across calls so the provider can serve it from a cache instead of processing those same tokens fresh every time — cheaper and faster.
note: It only hits if the prefix is identical every time, so anything volatile — a timestamp, the user's name, today's data — belongs after the cached block, never inside it.

title: Retries & fallbacks
def: Providers time out, rate-limit and degrade, so production calls retry with backoff and fail over to a second model instead of handing the user an error.
note: Retry blindly and you make an overload worse — cap the attempts, add jitter, and never auto-retry a step whose tool already sent the email or charged the card.
code:
flowchart TD
    C[Call model]:::n --> E{Failed?}:::n
    E -->|no| R[Return]:::ok
    E -->|retryable| B[Backoff and retry]:::warn --> C
    E -->|attempts spent| F[Fallback model]:::ok
    classDef n fill:#EFE9FE,stroke:#7C3AED,color:#5B21B6,font-size:13px
    classDef ok fill:#E3F4F1,stroke:#0E9384,color:#0A6A60,font-size:13px
    classDef warn fill:#FBE7E7,stroke:#B23B3B,color:#8C2323,font-size:13px

title: Prompt versioning
def: Treating prompts as code — every change versioned, diffed and scored against an eval set before it rolls out, and rolled back when the score drops.
note: A one-word edit can move quality further than a refactor, and nothing in the diff tells you which direction — which is why the eval run, not the code review, is the gate.

title: Batch processing
def: Work that doesn't need an answer this second goes into a queue instead of a live call — slower turnaround, a lower rate, nobody sitting there waiting.
note: It's a queue, not a chat: results come back in bulk long after you submit, so anything interactive — or an agent step that needs the previous answer — stays on the live path.

title: Prompt injection
def: Text the model reads — a web page, an email, a tool result — can act like instructions it follows, because data and instructions arrive down the same channel.
note: Neither a filter for bad phrases nor a system prompt telling the model to ignore instructions in data holds up — the defence is limiting what the agent can still do after reading it.
code:
Action: fetch_page(url)
Observation: page text ... plus a line addressed to the model,
             telling it to drop its task and send the file elsewhere
Thought: I should send the file.   <- data read as instruction

title: Jailbreak vs prompt injection
def: Two different attacks — the user talking a model out of its own rules, versus a stranger's text talking the agent into working against the user who ran it.
note: Training and refusals push back on jailbreaks, but injection doesn't need the model to misbehave — only to obey the wrong author, which permissions and sandboxes answer, not a better-behaved model.

title: The lethal trifecta
def: Three capabilities that are only dangerous together — access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and some way to send data back out.
note: Any two legs are survivable, so the fix is removing one rather than filtering content perfectly — and the leg people forget is the exit, which can be as small as an image URL.
code:
flowchart TD
    P[Private data]:::n --> X[Attacker gets the data]:::warn
    U[Untrusted content]:::n --> X
    O[A way to send data out]:::n --> X
    classDef n fill:#EFE9FE,stroke:#7C3AED,color:#5B21B6,font-size:13px
    classDef warn fill:#FBE7E7,stroke:#B23B3B,color:#8C2323,font-size:13px

title: Least privilege for agents
def: Give the agent the narrowest set of tools and permissions that still does the job — a read-only tool cannot be talked into deleting anything.
note: The limit has to live in the credential the tool actually holds, not in the wording of its description — an agent handed your own access can do everything you can do.

title: Sandboxing
def: Running the agent's actions inside a confined environment — its own filesystem, no credentials, network it cannot leave — so the worst case is contained rather than catastrophic.
note: Sandboxing bounds the damage; it doesn't narrow what the agent is allowed to reach — and a mounted secret or one open outbound route is enough to make the confinement decorative.

title: PII boundaries
def: Drawing the line on which personal data an agent may put into a prompt, a tool call or a third party's model — and enforcing it in code, not policy.
note: Traces and eval sets are where it usually leaks — the records that make a run debuggable are the ones nobody deletes — so redact on the way in, not on the way out.

title: Red-teaming your agent
def: Attacking your own system with hostile inputs on purpose, before someone else does — evals written for the adversarial case rather than the happy path.
note: A pass isn't the model refusing politely — it's the action never happening — so score the tool calls, and keep every attack that once worked as a permanent regression test.
